newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asia Metals - Zinc premiums slump in Singapore.
newsitem.headline: Asia Metals - Zinc premiums slump in Singapore.

text.p: Zinc premiums have plunged in Singapore due to the imminent arrival of some 30,000 tonnes of Chinese zinc destined for warehouses in the city-state, Far East base metal traders said on Friday.

"A couple of 10,000-tonne parcels are supposed to be on the way here. There's so much material becoming available, the premiums have come off," the general manager of a metal trading company told Reuters.
Premiums in Singapore for 25 kg zinc ingots slid to around US$10-$15 a tonne over London Metal Exchange (LME) cash prices from last week's $25-$30, dealers said.
One dealer said deals for zinc were done at $12.
"One can easily obtain material at $15," he said.
Another dealer said the "total figure coming in is about 30,000 tonnes. It's all from China."
"As the Chinese wave hits, premiums will definitely come down," a zinc industry official said.
What is aggravating the situation is the fact that around 10,000 tonnes of zinc were already in Singapore warehouses before reports of fresh Chinese zinc shipments emerged, dealers said.

"A lot of the zinc is not showing up on warrant," a dealer said, adding the total volume of the metal placed in warehouses in Singapore could eventually exceed 40,000 tonnes. "More material is expected to come in."
One trader said most of the zinc came from China's Zhuzhou Smelter. The metal was re-melted and is now being sold to take advantage of current high prices on the LME.
"I've heard of that report. The bottomline is that they'd rather sell it to traders rather than the LME," one dealer said.
Chinese zinc exports are expected to rise sharply this year with traders estimating they could reach as high as 350,000 to 400,000 tonnes against 210,000-220,000 tonnes in 1996.

"You'd get close to doubling their (Chinese zinc) exports because prices are so high," a dealer said, adding that low stocks and increasing consumption could turn 1998 "into one of the best years recently in zinc."
The only curious thing about the current situation, one dealer said, is the current direction of zinc prices on the LME when compared to the level of Singapore premiums.
"If the market is tight, premiums should be going up. But you don't see that in this market," the dealer said.
Three-month zinc was quoted by regional dealers at 0400 GMT at $1,375/79 a tonne, up from the close on the LME of $1,375.

In another development, aluminium premiums for third quarter supply contracts in Japan were finally set at $86-$90 CIF Japanese ports, up an average of five dollars from levels in the second quarter of 1997, dealers said.
"The talks were concluded this week in Japan. The final figure ranged between $86 and $90. Demand is going very well. That's why the premiums increased," a trader said.
Premiums for spot transactions in Japan, though, were running at around $95 CIF or higher, dealers said.
"Demand is so good I sold some Western material at $80-$85," an aluminium dealer said.
Premium levels in Korea were finalised at $90-$95 CIF Pusan, $90-$95 CIF Kaoshiung and Keelung. Premiums in Indonesia were pegged at $95-$100 CIF Jakarta.
-- Singapore Newsroom (65-8703305)
